title: Dave in Love Part Two
summary: Part Two resumes without a new introduction and first tests whether David Choe's phone relationship is meaningful despite never meeting. An unrelated story about a formerly known woman now reportedly homeless, using meth and being raped by a group is preserved as a secondhand allegation while protecting the vulnerable private person. The caller receives the alias Angel. David's therapist reportedly says he has never seemed happier; Asa asks whether distance permits feeling without ordinary relationship responsibility. David declares monogamy after one week and tells prior partners the sexual relationships are over. Bill Poon arrives dressed for a funeral on the wrong date, letting the room recap the story and revisit whether DVDASA helps anyone. Listener messages describe companionship during rehab or suicidal periods, but the cast weighs that against entertainment, exposure and the availability of real therapy. David describes crying, renewed concern for other people and buying unproven 'post-stroke' supplements for Angel's father. He and friends perform increasingly invasive identity checks. A Hawaii friend finally reverse-searches Angel's photos and identifies them as images of public model Jaclyn Swedberg. Angel later admits using another person's photos and says the deception went farther than intended. This establishes catfishing; it does not authenticate her name, alleged real photo, salon, ethnicity, family, father, stroke, charities, stalkers, cancer connections or social graph. David initially imagines violent retaliation, then calls his therapist and de-escalates. He knowingly keeps the fantasy going for one final day, falsely implies he knew all along, and sends novelty genital and body images as his own counter-deception. He admits beauty was central to his attraction, contradicting earlier claims that sex, body or gender would not matter. The trust breach, not the caller's ordinary appearance, becomes the reason he says a relationship is impossible. Crucially, he also acknowledges that she tried to stop on the first day and that he refused to let the contact end; the Part One panic and parking-lot vigil remain coercive pressure rather than retroactive romance. The cast debates cancer fraud, small-island exposure, fantasy, AI intimacy, chat-room deception, body dysmorphia, race and readiness for love. David considers meeting Angel or bringing her onto the show, but neither happens in this source. He offers to fund Valentin's education and returns to whether art can be created from peace rather than anger. Every idea, slur, contradiction and allegation remains attributable. Private identity trails and intimate images do not. Two empty zero-duration records are the only cleaner drops, and no named dialogue is published.
source_notes: Both cleaner removals are empty zero-duration records; raw and clean word counts are identical.
The three vocabulary repairs are supported: DVDASA twice and Her for the explicitly named Spike Jonze film.

This is continuous with Episode 131. The introduced participant set remains David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark and Steve Lee, with Bill Poon, Scrotum Coat and Alex joining or appearing later; zero turns/windows prohibits named dialogue.
Reverse-image evidence and the caller's reported admission establish that Jaclyn Swedberg's photos were misused. Jaclyn Swedberg is not the caller.
The caller's alleged real photo and biography are not independently authenticated. One confirmed deception does not validate or invalidate every other claim.

The private caller's name, phone, salon, social accounts, followers, relatives, exact locations, charity records, father health, hospital audio, stalker stories and pornography-work connections are excluded from identity discovery.
David acknowledges the caller tried to end contact on the first day and said not to force her. That continuity keeps the parking-lot wait and starvation/death threat in the coercion record.
The vulnerable formerly known woman at the opening is not identified. Homelessness, drug use and group rape are secondhand allegations, not a sexual-entertainment anecdote.
Cancer, stroke, sociopathy, addiction and body-dysmorphia claims remain attributed and unverified unless the episode itself supplies direct admission.
A possible future meeting or guest episode is discussed but does not occur here.
speaker_policy: Episode metadata may retain the known Part One participant set and note later arrivals, but zero diarized turns and zero identity windows prohibit line-level assignments to David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark, Steve Lee, Bill Poon, Alex, Scrotum Coat or any caller/private person.

chapters.title: Life Sucks Die and the show
she had asked him to stop

connections.why: Her supplies a vocabulary for real emotion attached to uncertain embodiment.
A secondhand rape/homelessness account should not become entertainment metadata or an identity trail.
Emotional improvement can be real even when beliefs about the other person are false.
Distance offers intimacy without many ordinary responsibilities or immediate bodily risk.
David ranks betrayal of a loved partner above crimes against strangers because the stated relationship intensifies duty.
Choosing exclusivity is distinct from claiming ownership of another person's body.
Crisis and rehab messages show perceived value but not clinical efficacy or causation.
Guessing stroke and buying supplements cannot substitute for emergency and rehabilitative care.
Legitimate doubt does not authorize publishing phone, family, workplace or follower graphs.
Individual deception allegations are generalized across porn performers without evidence.
David compares catfishing to paying for an immersive fiction that produces real feeling.
The show's value is judged against time for visual art and the psychological cost of radical disclosure.
Listeners may value hearing that other people are weird without sharing the cast's exact lives.
A virtual relationship can feel like full commitment while preserving distance and easy withdrawal.
Elaborate financial defenses contrast with voluntarily entering an unverifiable emotional relationship.
The image source proves photo misuse while requiring strict separation of public model and private caller.
Calling a therapist interrupts violent fantasy before action.
The admission that she tried to stop contact changes the interpretation of the earlier romanticized vigil.
David responds to catfishing with fake intimate images, complicating a simple victim/perpetrator story.
He revises his claim that body and identity would not matter once the stolen beauty is removed.
Small-island social density makes combined details unusually re-identifying and potentially ruinous.
Discovering deception does not automatically authorize publishing the deceiver's legal identity or intimate trail.
Readiness for commitment can turn the next plausible person into the imagined right person.
The episode's abstract helping question becomes a specific offer to fund education.
